web-design.application: A sample page uses a logical heading hierarchy rather than styling every section title as a generic paragraph.
web-design.check: Inspect structure and reading order as well as appearance.

web-design.title: Links and navigation
web-design.explanation: A link navigates to a destination; a button performs an action. Descriptive link text helps people predict where navigation leads.
web-design.application: 'View course outline' is more informative than several unrelated links all labeled 'Click here.'
web-design.check: Check the target, accessible name, focus state, and whether the behavior matches the control's purpose.

web-design.title: Images and alternatives
web-design.explanation: Alternative text conveys an image's relevant purpose; decorative images can have empty alternatives when appropriate. File names are rarely useful descriptions.
web-design.application: A meaningful event image needs information serving the page's task, while a purely decorative flourish should not add spoken clutter.
web-design.check: Decide what the image contributes in context and test the page without relying on the picture.

web-design.title: CSS selectors
web-design.explanation: CSS selectors identify elements to style; the cascade and specificity influence which declarations apply. A later rule does not always override a more specific earlier selector.
web-design.application: A class-based style and an element style can compete, so inspect the actual matched rules before adding more overrides.
web-design.check: Change the smallest relevant rule and check the effect in other components.

web-design.title: Spacing and hierarchy
web-design.explanation: Spacing and hierarchy should communicate grouping, sequence, and emphasis. Consistency helps people recognize equivalent items rather than treating every block as a new pattern.
web-design.application: A fictional set of course cards aligns titles, descriptions, and actions using shared spacing rather than manual offsets.
web-design.check: Check long titles and unequal content lengths, not only one ideal card.

web-design.title: Responsive layouts
web-design.explanation: Responsive layout adapts to available space and content needs. A fixed width that works on one desktop can overflow a smaller screen.
web-design.application: A sample two-column layout becomes one column when the content no longer fits comfortably.
web-design.check: Test narrow widths, text enlargement, and actual long content without hiding necessary information.

web-design.title: Color and contrast
web-design.explanation: Contrast compares foreground and background luminance, not how bright either color looks alone. Text over an image can vary in contrast across the same area.
web-design.application: A dark label on a changing photograph is checked at its actual placement rather than on a plain color sample.
web-design.check: Measure the applicable WCAG criterion and inspect hover, focus, error, and disabled states separately.

web-design.title: Forms and labels
web-design.explanation: A form control needs a persistent accessible label; placeholder text alone is inadequate. Errors should identify the problem and help the user recover.
web-design.application: A fictional email field retains its label after entry and explains an invalid value without clearing unrelated answers.
web-design.check: Associate labels and instructions with controls, and test keyboard and error handling.

web-design.title: Keyboard navigation
web-design.explanation: Keyboard users need reachable controls, visible focus, and a logical order. A clickable element is not automatically keyboard-operable.
web-design.application: A fictional menu can be opened, navigated, and closed without a mouse and without trapping focus.
web-design.check: Test the whole task using the keyboard rather than checking only whether the first link receives focus.

web-design.title: Content clarity
web-design.explanation: Clear content names the action, requirements, and likely result in the user's language. A technically accurate message may still be unhelpful if it hides the next step.
web-design.application: A sample error explains which field needs attention and preserves completed work.
web-design.check: Check comprehension with the intended task and avoid relying only on color or jargon.

web-design.title: Performance basics
web-design.explanation: Page performance includes loading, rendering, and responsiveness, not just one file's size. Oversized media and unnecessary work can delay the task.
web-design.application: A fictional landing page uses appropriately sized images instead of loading a full-resolution original for a small card.
web-design.check: Measure under representative device and network conditions before declaring the page fast.

web-design.title: Publishing concepts
web-design.explanation: A domain identifies a name, DNS helps resolve it, hosting serves content, and HTTPS protects transport. Configuring one does not automatically complete the others.
web-design.application: A successful local preview does not prove the deployed domain resolves to the intended current version.
web-design.check: Check the actual public URL, certificate behavior, routes, and deployed content.

web-design.title: Page testing
web-design.explanation: Page testing should cover navigation, forms, content, responsive behavior, keyboard access, and errors. A passing automated check does not replace task-based manual review.
web-design.application: A fictional test includes an invalid form entry and a narrow screen rather than only opening the home page.
web-design.check: Record expected result, observed behavior, device conditions, and unresolved issues.

web-design.title: Portfolio project
web-design.explanation: A web portfolio should explain audience, task, implementation choices, accessibility checks, and limits. A screenshot alone does not show whether the experience works.
web-design.application: A fictional case study includes a usable page and a brief account of testing, without claiming universal compliance.
web-design.check: Use authorized assets, protect private data, and describe your actual contribution accurately.

javascript-foundations.title: Programs and instructions
javascript-foundations.explanation: A program executes instructions according to language rules and the runtime environment. The order of operations and available inputs affect the output.
javascript-foundations.application: In a simple fictional script, printing a value before changing it produces a different result from changing it first.
javascript-foundations.check: Trace each statement and predict the output before running safe sample code.

javascript-foundations.title: Variables and values
javascript-foundations.explanation: A variable binds a name to a value; let permits reassignment, while const prevents reassignment of that binding. Const does not make an object's contents universally immutable.
javascript-foundations.application: A sample count declared with let can increase; a const object may still have an editable property.
javascript-foundations.check: Distinguish rebinding from changing an object's contents.

javascript-foundations.title: Data types
javascript-foundations.explanation: Numbers, strings, booleans, undefined, and null have different meanings. Automatic conversion can produce results that look surprising when types are not explicit.
javascript-foundations.application: The expression '2' + 3 produces text '23', while 2 + 3 produces the number 5.
javascript-foundations.check: Check the intended type at an input boundary rather than trusting appearance.

javascript-foundations.title: Operators
javascript-foundations.explanation: Operators perform arithmetic, comparison, assignment, and other operations. Strict equality avoids the type conversion performed by loose equality in many comparisons.
javascript-foundations.application: In a sample check, '5' === 5 is false because the types differ.
javascript-foundations.check: Use parentheses when needed to make evaluation order clear and test both expected types.

javascript-foundations.title: Conditions
javascript-foundations.explanation: A condition selects a path based on an expression's result. Boundary values often reveal whether a comparison matches the stated rule.
javascript-foundations.application: If a fictional requirement is age >= 18, test 17, 18, and 19 rather than only an obviously eligible value.
javascript-foundations.check: Write the rule in plain language and compare the boundary tests with that rule.

javascript-foundations.title: Arrays
javascript-foundations.explanation: An array is an ordered collection with zero-based indexing. Its length is a count, so the last existing index is normally one less than that length.
javascript-foundations.application: A three-item sample has indices 0, 1, and 2; requesting index 3 does not retrieve a fourth existing item.
javascript-foundations.check: Check empty arrays and avoid assuming an element exists at every requested index.

javascript-foundations.title: Loops
javascript-foundations.explanation: A loop repeats work while its continuation condition allows it. Incorrect conditions can skip items, repeat too many times, or never terminate.
javascript-foundations.application: For a three-item array, a typical index-based traversal stops before the index equals length.
javascript-foundations.check: Use small safe datasets and verify start, stop, and update conditions before wider use.

javascript-foundations.title: Functions
javascript-foundations.explanation: A function groups behavior, receives parameters, and may return a value. Printing a result and returning it to the caller are different operations.
javascript-foundations.application: A sample add function returns 2 + 3 so another expression can use 5, rather than only showing it in a console.
javascript-foundations.check: Test inputs and returned outputs separately from display behavior.

javascript-foundations.title: Objects
javascript-foundations.explanation: Objects associate property names with values. A missing property can yield undefined, which is different from a confirmed value of zero or an empty string.
javascript-foundations.application: A fictional user object with a name but no phone property should not be treated as a verified blank phone record.
javascript-foundations.check: Check the required properties before using them and avoid exposing personal data in examples.

javascript-foundations.title: Input validation
javascript-foundations.explanation: Input validation checks type, allowed range, required fields, and format before processing. Converting text to a number does not prove that the number is valid for the task.
javascript-foundations.application: A fictional quantity accepts a finite positive integer and rejects empty text, negative values, and nonnumeric input.
javascript-foundations.check: Validate on the trusted processing side as well as improving feedback in the interface.

javascript-foundations.title: DOM concepts
javascript-foundations.explanation: The DOM represents a document as objects that scripts can inspect and change. Selecting an element can fail when it does not exist or the document is not ready.
javascript-foundations.application: A sample script checks whether its target was found before changing the displayed text.
javascript-foundations.check: Use appropriate text APIs for plain text and do not insert untrusted content as HTML.

javascript-foundations.title: Events
javascript-foundations.explanation: An event signals something such as a click, input change, or form submission. Registering a handler is different from immediately calling the function.
javascript-foundations.application: A sample button invokes its handler when the event occurs rather than during setup.
javascript-foundations.check: Check the event target, required default behavior, and whether repeated registration causes duplicate work.

javascript-foundations.title: Debugging
javascript-foundations.explanation: Debugging compares expected with observed behavior and narrows the cause through evidence. An error message identifies a useful starting point, not always the complete explanation.
javascript-foundations.application: A fictional function is tested with one small input while intermediate values and assumptions are examined.
javascript-foundations.check: Change one relevant factor and rerun the failing case before declaring the defect corrected.

javascript-foundations.title: Testing cases
javascript-foundations.explanation: Tests should include normal, boundary, empty, and invalid cases relevant to the specification. A single successful example cannot establish correct general behavior.
javascript-foundations.application: A sample total function is tested with no items, one item, multiple items, and an invalid value.
javascript-foundations.check: State the expected result before observing the actual output.

javascript-foundations.title: Coding project
javascript-foundations.explanation: A small coding project should solve a defined task with explicit inputs, outputs, validation, and test cases. More features do not automatically provide better evidence of understanding.
javascript-foundations.application: A fictional checklist app documents how adding, editing, and removing an item should behave.
javascript-foundations.check: Use safe sample data and explain both known limitations and your own implementation choices.

data-spreadsheets.title: Data questions
data-spreadsheets.explanation: A data question needs a defined population, period, measure, and intended decision. Collecting more rows does not compensate for an unclear question.
data-spreadsheets.application: 'How many completed appointments occurred each week?' requires a completion definition and time range.
data-spreadsheets.check: Write the decision and measure before choosing columns or formulas.

data-spreadsheets.title: Rows and columns
data-spreadsheets.explanation: A row should represent a consistent unit of observation and columns should describe that unit. Mixing totals with individual records can distort later calculations.
data-spreadsheets.application: A fictional attendance table keeps one participant-session per row rather than adding unlabeled subtotal rows among entries.
data-spreadsheets.check: Identify the row's meaning and preserve it during sorting and filtering.

data-spreadsheets.title: Field definitions
data-spreadsheets.explanation: A field definition states meaning, type, unit, valid values, and any coding rule. Two similarly named columns can represent different measures.
data-spreadsheets.application: 'Amount' is clarified as dollars paid before fees during the reporting period, rather than a mix of charges and receipts.
data-spreadsheets.check: Keep a short data dictionary with the dataset.

data-spreadsheets.title: Data entry checks
data-spreadsheets.explanation: Entry checks reduce preventable errors by controlling required values, formats, and ranges. They do not guarantee that a plausible-looking value is true.
data-spreadsheets.application: A fictional date field rejects text in the wrong format while source verification still checks the actual appointment date.
data-spreadsheets.check: Use both validation and a check against the original source.

data-spreadsheets.title: Cleaning duplicates
data-spreadsheets.explanation: A duplicate depends on the record definition and relevant identifiers, not simply matching one cell. Removing repeated names can delete legitimate separate events.
data-spreadsheets.application: Two sessions attended by the same person are not necessarily duplicate attendance records.
data-spreadsheets.check: Define the duplicate key and preserve an original copy before cleaning.

data-spreadsheets.title: Missing values
data-spreadsheets.explanation: Missing, zero, and not applicable represent different situations. Replacing every blank with zero can change averages and imply events that never occurred.
data-spreadsheets.application: A fictional missing payment amount remains flagged as unknown rather than counted as a confirmed zero-dollar payment.
data-spreadsheets.check: Document the missing-value rule and its effect on the result.

data-spreadsheets.title: Useful formulas
data-spreadsheets.explanation: SUM, COUNT, and AVERAGE answer different questions and can treat blanks or text differently. A formula needs the intended range and unit.
data-spreadsheets.application: A practice total of 10, 20, and 30 is 60; the average is 20, and the record count is three.
data-spreadsheets.check: Check a small known sample and inspect the referenced cells before trusting a large range.

data-spreadsheets.title: Conditional logic
data-spreadsheets.explanation: Conditional logic translates a rule into separate outcomes. Boundary wording such as 'at least' or 'greater than' changes the correct comparison.
data-spreadsheets.application: A fictional threshold of at least 80 includes 80, while a rule greater than 80 does not.
data-spreadsheets.check: Test a value below, equal to, and above the threshold.

data-spreadsheets.title: Lookup concepts
data-spreadsheets.explanation: A lookup matches a key to information in another range. Exact matching, duplicates, missing keys, and the return range affect the result.
data-spreadsheets.application: Two fictional customers with the same surname show why a unique authorized identifier can be more reliable than name alone.
data-spreadsheets.check: Test a known match, a missing key, and a duplicate-key case.

data-spreadsheets.title: Pivot summaries
data-spreadsheets.explanation: A pivot summary groups records and aggregates a selected measure. Count and sum are different calculations, and source updates may require refresh.
data-spreadsheets.application: A fictional weekly attendance summary counts sessions rather than adding participant identification numbers.
data-spreadsheets.check: Verify the source range, grouping, aggregation, filters, and refresh state.

data-spreadsheets.title: Charts and scales
data-spreadsheets.explanation: Chart scales, units, grouping, and missing categories affect interpretation. Different axes can make equal-looking changes represent different amounts.
data-spreadsheets.application: A sample bar chart compares weekly totals on a consistent axis instead of starting each bar from a different baseline.
data-spreadsheets.check: Show the relevant period and source, and check that the visual supports the actual comparison.

data-spreadsheets.title: Percentages
data-spreadsheets.explanation: A percentage needs a numerator and denominator referring to the same defined population. Percentage-point change differs from relative percentage change.
data-spreadsheets.application: An increase from 20% to 30% is ten percentage points and a 50% relative increase from the original 20%.
data-spreadsheets.check: State which change is being reported and verify the denominator.

data-spreadsheets.title: Privacy and minimization
data-spreadsheets.explanation: Data minimization limits collection to what the task needs. Removing direct names does not always eliminate identification risk when other fields can be combined.
data-spreadsheets.application: A fictional public summary uses grouped counts instead of a list of identifiable participants and sensitive details.
data-spreadsheets.check: Check authorized purpose, access, retention, and disclosure before collecting or sharing data.

data-spreadsheets.title: Findings and limits
data-spreadsheets.explanation: A finding should state what the records support and what they cannot establish. Association or a before-and-after difference alone does not prove causation.
data-spreadsheets.application: A fictional attendance increase is reported alongside changes in schedule or recruitment that could also explain it.
data-spreadsheets.check: Separate observation, possible explanation, limitation, and next verification step.

data-spreadsheets.title: Data project
data-spreadsheets.explanation: A data project needs a defined question, trustworthy source, consistent fields, documented cleaning, checked calculation, and an understandable result.
data-spreadsheets.application: A fictional project retains its original data and records how missing entries affected the summary.
data-spreadsheets.check: Use authorized sample data and explain limitations instead of presenting an estimate as a measured fact.

responsible-ai.title: What AI generates
responsible-ai.explanation: Generative AI produces outputs using learned patterns and context. Fluent language and realistic formatting are not evidence that a factual claim or citation is correct.
responsible-ai.application: A fictional answer naming a nonexistent report is checked against the publisher's actual website.
responsible-ai.check: Treat output as a draft requiring verification, not as an independently authoritative source.

responsible-ai.title: Task suitability
responsible-ai.explanation: Task suitability depends on consequences, available evidence, privacy, and review capacity. Low-risk drafting differs from an irreversible or consequential decision.
responsible-ai.application: A fictional brainstorming task is suitable for reviewable suggestions, while an employment decision requires the approved human process.
responsible-ai.check: Choose a task whose output can be checked and corrected before use.

responsible-ai.title: Clear prompts
responsible-ai.explanation: A useful prompt names the task, relevant context, constraints, and desired output. More instructions cannot guarantee truth or remove the need to inspect results.
responsible-ai.application: A fictional request asks for a concise draft using only supplied facts and explicitly marks missing information.
responsible-ai.check: Do not add confidential data merely to make a prompt more specific.

responsible-ai.title: Source verification
responsible-ai.explanation: A citation must lead to a real source that supports the precise claim. A working link or recognizable publisher name alone does not establish that support.
responsible-ai.application: A learner opens a fictional cited report, locates the stated finding, and checks its date and scope.
responsible-ai.check: Verify facts against primary sources and distinguish direct evidence from an inference.

responsible-ai.title: Privacy boundaries
responsible-ai.explanation: Prompts and files can contain personal or organizational information. Tool approval, retention, access, and contractual controls matter before data is entered.
responsible-ai.application: A fictional support draft uses an invented customer and redacted issue instead of a real account record.
responsible-ai.check: Use only approved tools and minimum necessary data, and follow the organization's privacy requirements.

responsible-ai.title: Editing drafts
responsible-ai.explanation: Editing an AI draft means checking meaning, factual accuracy, tone, omissions, and audience suitability. Correct grammar does not establish correct content.
responsible-ai.application: A fictional message is revised after the model invents a commitment the sender never made.
responsible-ai.check: Compare every factual statement and promised action with the actual source material.

responsible-ai.title: Learning with AI
responsible-ai.explanation: AI can support practice by offering examples or explanations, but learning requires the learner to inspect reasoning and try the task. Repetition of an answer is not proof of understanding.
responsible-ai.application: A learner predicts a small code sample's output, runs safe tests, and checks the result against official documentation.
responsible-ai.check: Explain the reasoning independently and verify important points outside the AI conversation.

responsible-ai.title: Bias and assumptions
responsible-ai.explanation: Bias can enter through training data, input assumptions, missing context, and output use. Neutral-sounding language does not establish fairness across people or groups.
responsible-ai.application: A fictional job description is reviewed for assumptions unrelated to actual role requirements.
responsible-ai.check: Use the approved review process and ask who may be excluded or misrepresented.

responsible-ai.title: Job-search support
responsible-ai.explanation: AI can help organize truthful job-search material but should not fabricate qualifications, experience, references, or employer facts. A tailored resume still needs the applicant's verification.
responsible-ai.application: A fictional draft strengthens the wording of a real responsibility without inventing a numerical result.
responsible-ai.check: Compare every claim with actual evidence and confirm the employer's requirements and submission channel.

responsible-ai.title: Spreadsheet assistance
responsible-ai.explanation: An AI-generated spreadsheet formula must match the application, data structure, ranges, and intended rule. A formula that runs can still calculate the wrong quantity.
responsible-ai.application: A fictional formula is checked on three known records, including an empty or boundary case.
responsible-ai.check: Verify results manually on a small sample and protect sensitive workbook data.

responsible-ai.title: Creative rights
responsible-ai.explanation: Generated material can raise rights, provenance, trademark, and likeness questions. Tool access or a subscription does not settle every right to publish or reuse an output.
responsible-ai.application: A fictional marketing draft is checked for unauthorized brand claims and assets before distribution.
responsible-ai.check: Review applicable tool terms and source permissions; obtain qualified advice where rights are uncertain.

responsible-ai.title: Automation boundaries
responsible-ai.explanation: Automation can turn a mistaken output into repeated or irreversible actions. Approval boundaries and rollback matter more as consequences increase.
responsible-ai.application: A fictional workflow prepares a draft for review rather than automatically sending messages or approving payments.
responsible-ai.check: Keep consequential actions behind the authorized human decision and test with safe data first.

responsible-ai.title: Recognizing uncertainty
responsible-ai.explanation: An uncertain answer can still sound confident. Missing information should be exposed rather than replaced by a plausible guess or unsupported probability.
responsible-ai.application: A fictional response says which required fact is unknown and identifies the official place to confirm it.
responsible-ai.check: Ask what evidence is missing and stop short of a claim that the evidence cannot support.

responsible-ai.title: Output evaluation
responsible-ai.explanation: Evaluation should compare output with explicit criteria such as correctness, completeness, safety, privacy, and task relevance. Preference for the writing style is only one dimension.
responsible-ai.application: Two fictional drafts are scored against the same factual checklist instead of choosing the more persuasive-sounding version.
responsible-ai.check: Keep examples of failures and retest after changing the prompt or tool.

responsible-ai.title: Responsible workflow
responsible-ai.explanation: A responsible workflow assigns an owner to input selection, output verification, approval, and records. Responsibility is not transferred to a model because it generated the content.
responsible-ai.application: A fictional process saves the source facts, reviewed draft, reviewer decision, and final approved action.
responsible-ai.check: Use a repeatable check and revisit the process when the task or tool changes.

reentry-planning.title: A realistic first week
reentry-planning.explanation: A first-week plan should distinguish immediate essentials, fixed obligations, and tasks that depend on another service. Many resources require eligibility checks or appointments before they can help.
reentry-planning.application: A fictional plan secures a reachable contact method and confirms required appointments before scheduling several optional visits.
reentry-planning.check: Mark each item confirmed, pending, or dependent on another step rather than treating every goal as available today.

reentry-planning.title: Documents and identity
reentry-planning.explanation: Identity and release documentation can be needed for services, but required evidence varies by agency. One document is not guaranteed to satisfy every application.
reentry-planning.application: A learner lists the issuing agency, exact required document, acceptable alternatives, and the next official contact.
reentry-planning.check: Check the agency's current instructions and protect originals and copies; do not send sensitive documents to unverified contacts.

reentry-planning.title: Appointment planning
reentry-planning.explanation: An appointment plan includes purpose, location, arrival requirements, travel, documents, and an authorized contact if something changes. A calendar entry alone does not establish readiness.
reentry-planning.application: A fictional 10 a.m. visit includes time to arrive, complete intake, and travel onward rather than scheduling the next task at 10:15.
reentry-planning.check: Confirm the instructions and build a realistic buffer without assuming every office accepts late arrival.

reentry-planning.title: Transportation options
reentry-planning.explanation: Transportation planning should compare route, schedule, cost, accessibility, and a permitted backup. A route available on weekdays may not operate the same way on weekends.
reentry-planning.application: A learner checks the actual arrival window for a training session and records an alternate contact if the ride fails.
reentry-planning.check: Verify service through the current provider and notify the appointment office early when a barrier appears.

reentry-planning.title: A reachable contact method
reentry-planning.explanation: A contact method needs to be usable and checked, not merely listed on a form. Service teams may be unable to reach an inactive number or full voicemail.
reentry-planning.application: A fictional routine checks messages at a chosen time and records which office requires a return call.
reentry-planning.check: Confirm that messages can be received and keep account recovery and private contact information secure.

reentry-planning.title: Daily structure
reentry-planning.explanation: Daily structure works best when essentials and realistic breaks have space alongside obligations. An overfilled schedule can turn one delay into several missed commitments.
reentry-planning.application: A fictional day uses a few anchor tasks and leaves travel and meal time between them.
reentry-planning.check: Review what actually fit and adjust the plan rather than interpreting a crowded schedule as a personal failure.

reentry-planning.title: Service navigation
reentry-planning.explanation: Service navigation separates a referral from eligibility, intake, approval, and actual delivery. Being given a resource name does not mean a place or benefit is confirmed.
reentry-planning.application: A learner asks a program what documents are needed, when intake occurs, and how to follow up.
reentry-planning.check: Record the response and identify an alternative if the service is unavailable or unsuitable.

reentry-planning.title: Tracking applications
reentry-planning.explanation: An application tracker connects the service or employer, date, confirmation, current status, missing item, and next action. 'Submitted' and 'approved' are different states.
reentry-planning.application: A fictional tracker shows one completed form awaiting a document and another application still under review.
reentry-planning.check: Use the actual confirmation and update dates instead of assuming silence means acceptance or rejection.

reentry-planning.title: Supervision communication
reentry-planning.explanation: Supervision requirements come from the person's actual conditions and authorized instructions. An employer, friend, or training provider cannot independently excuse or revise them.
reentry-planning.application: A fictional schedule conflict is raised promptly with the supervising authority through the required channel.
reentry-planning.check: Ask for clarification and retain authorized instructions; do not rely on a general course example as legal permission.

reentry-planning.title: Unexpected barriers
reentry-planning.explanation: A practical setback has observable facts and consequences, while a global conclusion about personal worth adds an interpretation. Separating them preserves room for action.
reentry-planning.application: When a ride cancels, the next task is to notify the office and explore permitted alternatives, not conclude that every plan is impossible.
reentry-planning.check: Name the barrier, immediate consequence, available option, and person who can authorize a change.

reentry-planning.title: Resource mapping
reentry-planning.explanation: A resource map links each need to a specific support, eligibility question, contact route, and backup. One person or organization rarely meets every need.
reentry-planning.application: A fictional map separates transport help, employment support, housing advice, and health-service navigation.
reentry-planning.check: Ask permission before assigning a personal supporter a role and verify that a listed service is currently available.

reentry-planning.title: Choosing priorities
reentry-planning.explanation: Prioritization compares deadlines, consequences, dependencies, and capacity. An important task can be blocked until an earlier document or appointment is completed.
reentry-planning.application: A learner chooses the next feasible document request instead of repeatedly revisiting a job application that requires that document.
reentry-planning.check: Explain why the selected task is both useful and possible now.

reentry-planning.title: Asking for help
reentry-planning.explanation: A clear request identifies the task, timing, kind of help, and what you will handle yourself. Specificity helps another person make an informed decision.
reentry-planning.application: A fictional request asks for a ride to one appointment or help identifying a route, rather than demanding unlimited transport.
reentry-planning.check: Allow the other person to decline and have an appropriate alternative where possible.

reentry-planning.title: Weekly review
reentry-planning.explanation: A weekly review should compare planned actions, actual outcomes, remaining barriers, and next adjustments. It is not simply a score of how motivated someone felt.
reentry-planning.application: A fictional review notes two appointments completed and one transport problem that needs a revised plan.
reentry-planning.check: Choose one practical change and retain evidence of progress without minimizing unresolved needs.

reentry-planning.title: A 30-day plan
reentry-planning.explanation: A 30-day plan should stage actions and include dependencies and alternatives. Housing, income, documents, health needs, and obligations may progress on different timelines.
reentry-planning.application: A fictional plan separates an application deadline from the unconfirmed date a service might become available.
reentry-planning.check: Review dates and current conditions rather than treating the original plan as a guaranteed sequence.

employment-readiness.title: Work goals
employment-readiness.explanation: A work goal should include tasks, required conditions, location, schedule, entry route, and essential constraints. Job title alone may hide a poor fit.
employment-readiness.application: A learner compares two fictional roles using actual commute and shift requirements before choosing applications.
employment-readiness.check: Separate nonnegotiable conditions from preferences and verify the employer's published requirements.

employment-readiness.title: Transferable skills
employment-readiness.explanation: Transferable skills become credible when tied to a truthful action and result. Informal, volunteer, or institutional experience should be described accurately without inventing employment.
employment-readiness.application: A fictional example describes organizing a recurring supply list and checking shortages rather than claiming an unearned manager title.
employment-readiness.check: Name what you did, how you did it, and what evidence supports the outcome.

employment-readiness.title: Reading job descriptions
employment-readiness.explanation: Required and preferred qualifications differ, but the employer determines eligibility. A vague resemblance to a role is not a substitute for reading the complete posting.
employment-readiness.application: A learner marks each requirement as met, unclear, or not yet met and identifies evidence for the first category.
employment-readiness.check: Ask through the official channel when a credential or condition is ambiguous.

employment-readiness.title: Resume structure
employment-readiness.explanation: A resume helps the employer find relevant evidence quickly. Accurate dates, clear responsibilities, and readable structure matter more than unsupported adjectives.
employment-readiness.application: A fictional bullet explains an actual task and verified result instead of saying only 'excellent worker.'
employment-readiness.check: Do not invent metrics, employers, credentials, or experience to fill a gap.

employment-readiness.title: Application accuracy
employment-readiness.explanation: Application accuracy requires checking each form's wording, dates, requested files, and required declarations. Copying an old answer can create an inconsistency.
employment-readiness.application: A fictional application asks for month and year while another asks for exact dates, so uncertain details are verified first.
employment-readiness.check: Review the final submission and retain an appropriate copy or confirmation securely.

employment-readiness.title: Explaining employment gaps
employment-readiness.explanation: Explaining a gap can be concise, truthful, and relevant to readiness now. A candidate can redirect to current skills without making a misleading statement.
employment-readiness.application: A fictional response names a period away from employment, describes current preparation, and returns to the role's actual requirements.
employment-readiness.check: Practice a version you can deliver accurately without unnecessary personal detail.

employment-readiness.title: Record-related questions
employment-readiness.explanation: Record-related questions depend on precise wording, the hiring process, and applicable law. There is no single disclosure script suitable for every job or jurisdiction.
employment-readiness.application: A learner pauses on an unclear question and seeks qualified local guidance instead of guessing what the employer is legally allowed to ask.
employment-readiness.check: Answer truthfully as required and verify disputed records through appropriate official channels.

employment-readiness.title: Interview examples
employment-readiness.explanation: An interview example should distinguish situation, responsibility, your actions, and outcome. The useful evidence is what you actually contributed, including what you learned.
employment-readiness.application: A fictional candidate explains how they clarified a task and met a deadline rather than taking credit for an entire team's work.
employment-readiness.check: Keep the story relevant, concise, and supportable under follow-up questions.

employment-readiness.title: Interview practice
employment-readiness.explanation: Interview practice develops listening, pacing, clarification, and concise evidence. Memorizing a script can make it harder to answer a question that changes.
employment-readiness.application: A learner pauses, restates an unclear question, and selects one relevant example instead of reciting an unrelated prepared story.
employment-readiness.check: Seek feedback on clarity and evidence rather than personality judgments.

employment-readiness.title: Employer research
employment-readiness.explanation: Employer research should confirm services, actual openings, application channel, and the role's expectations. A social post or recruitment message may be incomplete or fraudulent.
employment-readiness.application: A learner checks the employer's official website and prepares a specific question about duties or training.
employment-readiness.check: Verify unusual requests and do not pay or disclose sensitive information merely because a message promises a job.

employment-readiness.title: References
employment-readiness.explanation: A reference needs consent, current contact information, and a relevant understanding of your work. A person's willingness should not be assumed.
employment-readiness.application: A fictional candidate explains the role to a proposed reference and confirms which responsibilities that person can honestly discuss.
employment-readiness.check: Keep the reference informed and use their information only with permission.

employment-readiness.title: Workplace reliability
employment-readiness.explanation: Reliability combines realistic commitments, preparation, communication, and recovery when a barrier occurs. Promising an impossible arrival time does not demonstrate dependability.
employment-readiness.application: A learner checks the commute before accepting a shift and confirms the employer's absence or delay reporting process.
employment-readiness.check: Communicate early and distinguish a proposed alternative from an approved change.

employment-readiness.title: Handling rejection
employment-readiness.explanation: A rejection is an outcome from one process, not a complete measure of ability or future prospects. Reflection is useful when it identifies evidence and a manageable next action.
employment-readiness.application: A learner reviews whether the role matched their qualifications, notes available feedback, and schedules the next relevant application.
employment-readiness.check: Avoid inventing the employer's motives or turning one response into a universal conclusion.

employment-readiness.title: Offer evaluation
employment-readiness.explanation: An offer should be evaluated using expected hours, pay timing, deductions, travel costs, benefits, and conditions, not only an advertised hourly rate.
employment-readiness.application: A fictional higher-rate job has fewer confirmed hours and a longer commute, so the learner compares realistic net cash flow.
employment-readiness.check: Confirm written terms and seek qualified advice for legal or financial questions rather than relying on an illustrative calculation.

employment-readiness.title: Job-search operating plan
employment-readiness.explanation: A job-search operating plan includes research, targeted applications, follow-up, practice, and review. Effort measures should be distinguished from employer-controlled outcomes.
employment-readiness.application: A fictional week tracks verified applications and follow-ups rather than interpreting daily response counts as personal worth.
employment-readiness.check: Adjust based on evidence about fit and barriers, keeping goals realistic and truthful.

personal-finance.title: Money inventory
personal-finance.explanation: A money inventory separates cash and accessible balances, expected income, required payments, and uncertain amounts. Available money is different from credit or an unconfirmed future deposit.
personal-finance.application: A fictional balance includes $60 cash and $140 in an account, while next week's possible income remains separately marked.
personal-finance.check: Verify dates and amounts before treating a resource as available for a current bill.

personal-finance.title: Needs and priorities
personal-finance.explanation: Priorities depend on consequences and actual obligations, not whether a payment request is the loudest. Essential needs and legal requirements can constrain available choices.
personal-finance.application: A learner compares food, housing, transport, and an optional purchase against the same limited fictional balance.
personal-finance.check: List the consequences and contact the relevant provider early when a payment cannot be met.

personal-finance.title: Cash flow timing
personal-finance.explanation: Cash flow maps when money arrives and when it leaves. A positive monthly total can still hide a shortage before a particular due date.
personal-finance.application: A fictional payment due Wednesday cannot automatically be covered by income arriving Friday without an authorized arrangement or another available source.
personal-finance.check: Review dates as well as totals and confirm any change in terms with the provider.

personal-finance.title: Budget categories
personal-finance.explanation: Useful budget categories distinguish stable obligations, variable essentials, irregular costs, and optional spending. A category is useful only if transactions can be classified consistently.
personal-finance.application: A fictional plan puts a known annual fee into a separate irregular-expense line rather than forgetting it until renewal.
personal-finance.check: Compare actual transactions with the plan and adjust assumptions instead of hiding overages.

personal-finance.title: Payment tracking
personal-finance.explanation: Scheduled, sent, received, and posted payments describe different stages. A confirmation can establish submission without proving the provider has applied the payment.
personal-finance.application: A fictional tracker records the submission reference and later checks the provider's updated balance.
personal-finance.check: Keep evidence securely and resolve discrepancies through verified contact channels.

personal-finance.title: Bank account questions
personal-finance.explanation: Account comparison includes fees, access, minimum balances, deposit availability, overdraft arrangements, and applicable protection. A convenient app does not settle all these questions.
personal-finance.application: A learner compares two fictional fee schedules and asks what happens if the balance falls below the stated minimum.
personal-finance.check: Read the current terms and verify the actual institution and protection rather than trusting a marketing label.

personal-finance.title: Emergency buffers
personal-finance.explanation: An emergency buffer is money set aside for uncertainty, but the affordable amount depends on essentials and current obligations. Small deposits can support progress without guaranteeing security.
personal-finance.application: Four illustrative deposits of $5 create $20 before interest, fees, or withdrawals.
personal-finance.check: Choose an amount you can actually maintain and review access and account costs.

personal-finance.title: Debt inventory
personal-finance.explanation: A debt inventory should distinguish verified, disputed, unfamiliar, and already resolved items. A payment demand alone does not establish its accuracy.
personal-finance.application: A fictional list records creditor, claimed amount, due date, and verification status instead of treating every call as a confirmed debt.
personal-finance.check: Use official dispute and verification resources and seek qualified guidance when rights or legal action are involved.

personal-finance.title: Credit reports
personal-finance.explanation: A credit report and a credit score are different products. Reports can contain errors, and disputes should address specific information through the appropriate process.
personal-finance.application: A learner records an unfamiliar account, the relevant report section, and supporting evidence rather than paying for a promise to erase history.
personal-finance.check: Use the current official report and dispute instructions and retain correspondence securely.

personal-finance.title: Interest concepts
personal-finance.explanation: Simple interest and compounding describe different calculations. Rate, period, fees, balance, and payment schedule determine the actual cost of a product.
personal-finance.application: An illustrative $100 at 10% simple annual interest for one year adds $10 before fees; this is not a quote for a real loan.
personal-finance.check: Compare the actual written terms and total repayment rather than transferring a classroom formula to every product.

personal-finance.title: Predatory offers
personal-finance.explanation: Pressure, hidden repayment terms, advance-fee promises, and unusual payment demands warrant careful verification. Guaranteed approval language does not establish affordability or legitimacy.
personal-finance.application: A fictional offer is paused while the learner checks the provider and written total cost through independent sources.
personal-finance.check: Do not send money or personal information merely to test an uncertain offer.

personal-finance.title: Income records
personal-finance.explanation: Income records should distinguish gross pay, deductions, net pay, and the period covered. The bank deposit alone may not explain taxes, benefits, or other deductions.
personal-finance.application: A fictional statement with $500 gross and $80 deductions shows $420 net before considering any separately paid expenses.
personal-finance.check: Check the actual statement and use the employer's proper channel for unexplained items.

personal-finance.title: Spending triggers
personal-finance.explanation: A spending trigger links a situation, feeling, or cue with a purchase response. Noticing that sequence creates an opportunity to choose a different action.
personal-finance.application: A fictional learner identifies late-night shopping after a stressful shift and tries a planned pause before optional purchases.
personal-finance.check: Evaluate actual spending and needs rather than judging the person's character.

personal-finance.title: Financial conversations
personal-finance.explanation: A financial conversation is clearer when it names the issue, amount or date, effect, and specific request. Agreement should be distinguished from a proposal.
personal-finance.application: A fictional household discussion asks to review a due date and shared cost rather than making an accusation about responsibility.
personal-finance.check: Confirm what was agreed, who handles each step, and when to revisit it.

personal-finance.title: A 90-day money plan
personal-finance.explanation: A 90-day money plan should use verified balances, payment timing, realistic income, and review dates. Uncertain resources need alternatives, not optimistic treatment as cash.
personal-finance.application: A fictional plan stages one immediate bill action, a small affordable buffer, and a later records review.
personal-finance.check: Update the plan when actual amounts or dates change and seek qualified assistance for unresolved financial or legal issues.

relationships-boundaries.title: Relationship inventory
relationships-boundaries.explanation: A relationship inventory can distinguish supportive behavior, unresolved obligations, stressors, and limits. Closeness does not automatically establish safety or unlimited access.
relationships-boundaries.application: A learner maps what kinds of support are realistically available without assigning another person responsibilities they have not accepted.
relationships-boundaries.check: Use observable behavior and consent rather than labels or assumptions about what family members must provide.

relationships-boundaries.title: Listening before reacting
relationships-boundaries.explanation: Listening involves allowing the other person to finish, checking meaning, and distinguishing understanding from agreement. Preparing a rebuttal while they speak can miss the actual concern.
relationships-boundaries.application: A fictional response summarizes the concern and asks whether it was understood before proposing a solution.
relationships-boundaries.check: Check accuracy instead of claiming you already know the other person's intention.

relationships-boundaries.title: Naming needs
relationships-boundaries.explanation: A need, feeling, request, and demand are different forms of communication. A specific request allows another person to understand what action is being proposed.
relationships-boundaries.application: A learner changes 'you never support me' to a factual concern and a request for one scheduled conversation.
relationships-boundaries.check: Keep the request achievable and allow an honest response.

relationships-boundaries.title: Boundaries and control
relationships-boundaries.explanation: A boundary describes what you will do or permit within your control. It cannot guarantee that another person changes behavior or agrees with the limit.
relationships-boundaries.application: A fictional boundary says when the learner will end a hostile conversation rather than promising to make the other person calm.
relationships-boundaries.check: Choose an action you can carry out safely and do not use boundary language to justify coercion.

relationships-boundaries.title: Concise boundary scripts
relationships-boundaries.explanation: A concise boundary script can state the limit, a brief relevant reason, and an alternative when appropriate. Repeated explanations can turn the limit into an endless negotiation.
relationships-boundaries.application: A fictional response declines one request and offers a permitted time to discuss another option.
relationships-boundaries.check: Use clear language and avoid promising an alternative you cannot actually provide.

relationships-boundaries.title: Conflict pause
relationships-boundaries.explanation: A pause should interrupt escalation and include a safe, realistic plan for what happens next. Walking away without any later communication can leave a different problem unresolved.
relationships-boundaries.application: A fictional conversation is paused with a proposed return time, subject to safety and both people's willingness.
relationships-boundaries.check: A pause is not a demand to resume an unsafe interaction; prioritize appropriate support when safety is uncertain.

relationships-boundaries.title: Accountability language
relationships-boundaries.explanation: Accountability language identifies your action, its impact, and a repair step without attaching a global judgment to your identity. Explanation should not erase responsibility.
relationships-boundaries.application: A fictional apology names a missed commitment and a concrete correction rather than blaming the other person's reaction.
relationships-boundaries.check: Check whether the proposed repair addresses the actual impact and respects the other person's choice.

relationships-boundaries.title: Repairing trust
relationships-boundaries.explanation: Trust develops through consistent behavior, honest information, respected limits, and follow-through. An apology or one successful interaction does not establish that every concern is resolved.
relationships-boundaries.application: A learner makes one modest commitment they can keep rather than asking for immediate restoration of unrestricted access.
relationships-boundaries.check: Let evidence accumulate and accept that the other person controls their own participation.

relationships-boundaries.title: Forgiveness and access
relationships-boundaries.explanation: Forgiveness, reconciliation, contact, and access are different decisions. Choosing one does not require granting the others or ignoring continuing risk.
relationships-boundaries.application: A fictional person can release a grievance while still limiting contact or protecting private information.
relationships-boundaries.check: Avoid treating spiritual or family expectations as permission to override another person's safety or consent.

relationships-boundaries.title: Family expectations
relationships-boundaries.explanation: Family expectations can remain unspoken and conflict with actual capacity. Clarifying roles, resources, timing, and limits helps prevent mismatched assumptions.
relationships-boundaries.application: A fictional household agrees on specific chores and contact arrangements rather than assuming everyone understands 'help out.'
relationships-boundaries.check: Confirm what each person actually accepted and revisit agreements when circumstances change.

relationships-boundaries.title: Supportive friendships
relationships-boundaries.explanation: Supportive friendships can provide connection and encouragement while respecting boundaries and individual responsibility. One friend should not be expected to solve every practical or emotional need.
relationships-boundaries.application: A learner identifies different supports for transport, employment advice, and social connection.
relationships-boundaries.check: Ask permission, avoid overpromising, and diversify support rather than making one relationship carry every task.

relationships-boundaries.title: Communication channels
relationships-boundaries.explanation: Channel choice affects privacy, clarity, timing, and the ability to respond. A group chat may be unsuitable for a sensitive disagreement or personal record.
relationships-boundaries.application: A fictional learner asks for an appropriate private conversation rather than posting another person's situation in a shared thread.
relationships-boundaries.check: Agree on the channel and protect private information, including screenshots and forwarded messages.

relationships-boundaries.title: Recognizing unsafe dynamics
relationships-boundaries.explanation: Threats, coercion, controlling behavior, and fear require attention to safety rather than ordinary communication practice alone. A relationship label does not make harmful behavior acceptable.
relationships-boundaries.application: A fictional scenario distinguishes a disagreement from pressure that restricts another person's choices or access to support.
relationships-boundaries.check: Seek appropriate qualified support and avoid an exercise that requires confronting a potentially dangerous person.

relationships-boundaries.title: Keeping agreements
relationships-boundaries.explanation: An agreement is easier to maintain when action, owner, timing, and the response to a barrier are clear. A vague intention cannot be checked in the same way.
relationships-boundaries.application: A fictional commitment names a date and contact plan if transport fails instead of promising to 'do better.'
relationships-boundaries.check: Communicate a problem early and obtain agreement before treating a proposed change as accepted.

relationships-boundaries.title: Relationship practice plan
relationships-boundaries.explanation: A relationship practice plan should target one skill in an appropriate situation, with an observable check. It should not require disclosure or another person's cooperation to count as personal practice.
relationships-boundaries.application: A learner chooses to summarize a concern before replying and later reviews whether they understood it accurately.
relationships-boundaries.check: Use safe or hypothetical situations and adjust the plan based on what actually happened.

entrepreneurship.title: A customer problem
entrepreneurship.explanation: A customer problem should identify who experiences it, when it occurs, how it is handled now, and why a different solution would matter. Your enthusiasm is not evidence of demand.
entrepreneurship.application: A fictional cleaning idea targets one specific customer and recurring difficulty instead of claiming that everyone needs the service.
entrepreneurship.check: Verify the problem through appropriate customer research before spending heavily on a solution.

entrepreneurship.title: Customer conversations
entrepreneurship.explanation: Customer conversations should explore actual behavior and needs rather than solicit compliments. Questions about past purchases or current alternatives can be more useful than hypothetical approval.
entrepreneurship.application: A learner asks how a fictional customer currently handles the task, what it costs, and what remains inconvenient.
entrepreneurship.check: Separate what the customer said from the founder's interpretation and avoid pressuring for a desired answer.

entrepreneurship.title: Value proposition
entrepreneurship.explanation: A value proposition connects a defined customer need with a clear benefit and credible reason to choose the service. A slogan alone may not explain what is actually delivered.
entrepreneurship.application: A fictional service promises a specific scheduled result within its capacity rather than 'the best solution for everyone.'
entrepreneurship.check: Check that the benefit is understandable, supportable, and connected to the researched problem.

entrepreneurship.title: Skills and capacity
entrepreneurship.explanation: Capacity includes skills, time, equipment, money, and the ability to deliver consistently. Accepting more work than you can perform can damage trust and cash flow.
entrepreneurship.application: A fictional owner calculates available hours after travel and administration rather than selling every hour as customer work.
entrepreneurship.check: Identify which tasks need training, a partner, or qualified licensed assistance before offering them.

entrepreneurship.title: Competitor research
entrepreneurship.explanation: Competitor research compares customer segment, offering, price structure, access, and evidence of service. A low price does not reveal the competitor's costs or profitability.
entrepreneurship.application: A learner compares published offers and customer needs rather than copying another company's branding or unsupported claims.
entrepreneurship.check: Use lawful public information and distinguish observed facts from guesses about performance.

entrepreneurship.title: Startup costs
entrepreneurship.explanation: Startup costs include one-time expenses and recurring operating costs before income becomes dependable. Revenue, profit, and available cash are different quantities.
entrepreneurship.application: A fictional launch budget separates equipment purchase from monthly insurance, supplies, and communication expenses.
entrepreneurship.check: Use current quotes and label estimates; include a realistic cash requirement before assuming the business funds itself.

entrepreneurship.title: Pricing concepts
entrepreneurship.explanation: Price must be considered alongside direct costs, overhead, time, demand, and contribution to the business. A markup percentage differs from a profit margin percentage.
entrepreneurship.application: An illustrative item costing $20 and selling for $30 has $10 gross difference before overhead, a 50% markup on cost and about 33% margin on price.
entrepreneurship.check: Keep the calculation's denominator and excluded costs visible.

entrepreneurship.title: Small tests
entrepreneurship.explanation: A small test should state the assumption, limited offering, audience, cost, and evidence that would justify the next step. Interest alone is different from an actual purchase or repeat use.
entrepreneurship.application: A fictional pilot measures completed paid orders and delivery effort rather than counting only positive comments.
entrepreneurship.check: Set a spending limit and review criterion before interpreting the result.

entrepreneurship.title: Business structure questions
entrepreneurship.explanation: Business structure, registration, licensing, tax treatment, and insurance are related but separate decisions. Forming an entity does not authorize every activity or remove every personal responsibility.
entrepreneurship.application: A learner lists questions for the appropriate state agency and qualified adviser instead of assuming an LLC solves all risk.
entrepreneurship.check: Verify current requirements for the actual location and activity before trading.

entrepreneurship.title: Customer agreements
entrepreneurship.explanation: A customer agreement should clarify scope, price, payment timing, customer responsibilities, changes, cancellation, and acceptance. Unclear scope can create disputes even when the work is competent.
entrepreneurship.application: A fictional service quote states what is included and how additional work must be approved.
entrepreneurship.check: Use an appropriate written agreement and qualified advice for enforceability or legal uncertainty.

entrepreneurship.title: Money separation
entrepreneurship.explanation: Separating business and personal records helps track income, expenses, and obligations. A positive account balance alone does not establish profit or money available for personal use.
entrepreneurship.application: A fictional owner records an equipment purchase and customer receipt distinctly rather than treating both as unexplained account changes.
entrepreneurship.check: Use the required records and seek qualified accounting or tax guidance for the actual business.

entrepreneurship.title: Marketing clarity
entrepreneurship.explanation: Marketing should state the customer, offered result, relevant terms, and clear action without unsupported guarantees. A large audience does not establish conversion or customer fit.
entrepreneurship.application: A fictional message gives the service area and booking step instead of promising outcomes beyond the owner's control.
entrepreneurship.check: Verify claims, permissions, and actual service capacity before publishing.

entrepreneurship.title: Service delivery
entrepreneurship.explanation: Reliable delivery connects intake, scheduling, execution, quality check, customer communication, and records. A sale is not complete simply because payment was received.
entrepreneurship.application: A fictional service checklist includes confirming scope and obtaining the customer's acceptance through the agreed process.
entrepreneurship.check: Track missed commitments and address exceptions before they become repeated operating problems.

entrepreneurship.title: Feedback and improvement
entrepreneurship.explanation: Feedback becomes useful when it identifies a specific need, issue, or successful behavior and leads to a testable change. A single comment does not establish a universal market preference.
entrepreneurship.application: A learner separates a recurring scheduling complaint from one customer's unrelated personal preference.
entrepreneurship.check: Compare patterns with actual customer and delivery evidence before changing the whole offer.

entrepreneurship.title: Launch plan
entrepreneurship.explanation: A launch plan should connect verified demand, capacity, costs, requirements, delivery, and a review date. A launch date alone is not an operating plan.
entrepreneurship.application: A fictional plan starts with a manageable offering and defines what must be confirmed before accepting customer commitments.
entrepreneurship.check: Keep uncertain assumptions visible and stage spending and promises according to evidence.

housing-stability.title: Housing needs
housing-stability.explanation: Housing needs include affordability, location, access, household size, safety, and any program requirements. A visually attractive listing may fail an essential practical need.
housing-stability.application: A learner distinguishes a required accessible route or reachable commute from an optional design preference.
housing-stability.check: List essentials first and verify actual availability and eligibility through the responsible provider.

housing-stability.title: A housing budget
housing-stability.explanation: Housing affordability involves recurring rent and related costs plus initial move-in expenses. A monthly rent figure alone can conceal deposits, utilities, transport, or required fees.
housing-stability.application: A fictional comparison separates first-month cash needed from the later recurring monthly total.
housing-stability.check: Use written terms and realistic income timing; an illustrative budget is not a guarantee of eligibility or affordability.

housing-stability.title: Document preparation
housing-stability.explanation: An application packet should follow the provider's actual requirements and protect sensitive documents. Requirements can differ across properties and assistance programs.
housing-stability.application: A learner prepares a checklist of requested evidence and keeps uncertain requirements for verification rather than sending every document available.
housing-stability.check: Confirm the recipient and permitted submission method before sharing identity or financial records.

housing-stability.title: Search sources
housing-stability.explanation: Housing search sources include verified property contacts, housing authorities, approved counselors, and relevant community programs. A referral is different from an available unit.
housing-stability.application: A fictional search log records where the lead came from, the official contact, status, and next action.
housing-stability.check: Recheck availability and qualification requirements rather than treating a resource listing as a confirmed placement.

housing-stability.title: Listing scams
housing-stability.explanation: Rental scammers can copy legitimate photos and listings while replacing contact details. Urgency and requests for hard-to-reverse payment before verification are important warning signs.
housing-stability.application: A fictional renter independently checks the property contact and proposed agreement instead of accepting a remote stranger's payment deadline.
housing-stability.check: Do not transfer money or sensitive records merely to prove interest in an unverified listing.

housing-stability.title: Application questions
housing-stability.explanation: An application question should be read exactly and answered accurately as required. Screening rules and available protections depend on the situation and applicable law.
housing-stability.application: A learner seeks qualified local guidance on an unclear question instead of using a universal disclosure script from another jurisdiction.
housing-stability.check: Verify current policy and preserve the actual written request and response.

housing-stability.title: Comparing options
housing-stability.explanation: Comparing housing options requires total cost, condition, transport, terms, eligibility, and practical access. A lower advertised rent can still create a less workable overall arrangement.
housing-stability.application: A fictional option with a long costly commute is compared with a higher-rent option using the same monthly assumptions.
housing-stability.check: Keep verified costs separate from unknowns and record the tradeoffs important to the household.

housing-stability.title: Lease vocabulary
housing-stability.explanation: A lease describes contractual rights and responsibilities such as payment, term, occupancy, access, maintenance, and changes. Familiar words can have specific legal effects.
housing-stability.application: A learner identifies the due date, late-payment language, notice procedure, and maintenance contact in a fictional agreement.
housing-stability.check: Read the full document and seek qualified local advice about unclear or disputed provisions before signing.

housing-stability.title: Move-in records
housing-stability.explanation: Move-in records establish observed condition and communications at the start of occupancy. A record is more useful when it identifies location, date, and the reported issue.
housing-stability.application: A fictional checklist separates an existing stain from damage that appeared after occupancy and records the submitted notice.
housing-stability.check: Follow the agreement's process and protect copies; a private note alone may not satisfy required notice.

housing-stability.title: Communicating maintenance
housing-stability.explanation: Maintenance communication should state location, symptom, timing, urgency, and the approved access arrangement. Reporting a problem is different from authorizing your own repair or withholding payment.
housing-stability.application: A fictional notice describes recurring water near a fixture and asks for the proper inspection process.
housing-stability.check: Use applicable emergency and written-notice procedures and seek qualified advice for unresolved legal questions.

housing-stability.title: Shared housing agreements
housing-stability.explanation: Shared housing works better when costs, chores, guests, privacy, quiet periods, and conflict procedures are explicit. A household agreement does not necessarily replace the lease or law.
housing-stability.application: A fictional household assigns specific chores and payment dates instead of assuming that everyone interprets 'share fairly' the same way.
housing-stability.check: Confirm consent and compatibility with actual lease requirements before treating the agreement as settled.

housing-stability.title: Neighborhood resources
housing-stability.explanation: Neighborhood stability depends partly on practical access to food, transport, health services, work, and supportive community resources. A nearby address does not prove a service is accessible or available.
housing-stability.application: A learner maps an actual route and opening time instead of listing a resource solely by distance.
housing-stability.check: Verify eligibility, accessibility, operating hours, and the current contact route.

housing-stability.title: Emergency alternatives
housing-stability.explanation: An emergency alternative may involve a shelter, housing service, trusted support, or another authorized option, but capacity and eligibility can change. A resource name is not a reserved place.
housing-stability.application: A fictional backup plan records when to contact the service and what confirmation is needed.
housing-stability.check: Use current local providers and appropriate qualified support rather than relying on an old availability claim.

housing-stability.title: Keeping records
housing-stability.explanation: Housing records can include the agreement, payments, notices, maintenance requests, condition reports, and contacts. Organization matters because a missing document can weaken follow-up.
housing-stability.application: A fictional folder separates submitted requests from responses and keeps dates and references visible.
housing-stability.check: Store private records securely and follow the relevant retention and communication process.

housing-stability.title: Housing stability plan
housing-stability.explanation: A stability plan connects recurring costs, deadlines, maintenance, communication, and backup options. It should identify early signals that a commitment may become difficult.
housing-stability.application: A fictional monthly review checks payment timing and upcoming changes before a missed obligation occurs.
housing-stability.check: Contact the relevant provider early and seek qualified help when a barrier or dispute exceeds what the plan can resolve.

stress-resilience.title: Stress signals
stress-resilience.explanation: Stress can show up through changes in attention, mood, physical tension, sleep, or behavior. A single sign does not establish a diagnosis or its cause.
stress-resilience.application: A fictional learner notes when concentration changes and what else was happening instead of labeling themselves as incapable.
stress-resilience.check: Observe patterns and seek qualified support for persistent, worsening, or concerning symptoms.

stress-resilience.title: Triggers and context
stress-resilience.explanation: A trigger is a situation or cue associated with a response, not necessarily the sole cause. Context, sleep, demands, and prior experiences can affect what follows.
stress-resilience.application: A learner separates a delayed message from the interpretation that the sender is deliberately rejecting them.
stress-resilience.check: Record the event, thought, feeling, and action as different parts of the sequence.

stress-resilience.title: Pause and notice
stress-resilience.explanation: A pause creates room to notice what is happening and choose an appropriate next action. It is not a requirement to remove a feeling before acting responsibly.
stress-resilience.application: A fictional learner notices rising frustration, stops a nonurgent reply, and identifies what needs clarification.
stress-resilience.check: Use a safe setting and choose an external attention task if inward attention is uncomfortable.

stress-resilience.title: Grounding attention
stress-resilience.explanation: Grounding can involve noticing present surroundings rather than trying to suppress every thought. Mindfulness exercises are optional and do not suit everyone in every situation.
stress-resilience.application: A learner notices a neutral object's color and location, then returns to one manageable task without demanding a calm feeling.
stress-resilience.check: Skip or stop an uncomfortable exercise; this is not treatment or a substitute for qualified support.

stress-resilience.title: Managing overload
stress-resilience.explanation: Overload can reflect too many demands, unclear priorities, insufficient recovery, or missing resources. Adding motivation language does not resolve every practical barrier.
stress-resilience.application: A fictional task list is narrowed to one necessary next action while another request is clarified or deferred appropriately.
stress-resilience.check: Compare demands with actual capacity and seek support rather than assuming effort alone removes the constraint.

stress-resilience.title: Sleep-supporting routines
stress-resilience.explanation: Sleep-supporting routines can include consistent timing and a suitable environment, but ongoing sleep problems can have multiple causes. A schedule is not a diagnosis or guaranteed remedy.
stress-resilience.application: A learner identifies one adjustable evening habit and observes whether it helps without promising a fixed result.
stress-resilience.check: Seek qualified advice for persistent sleep difficulty or impairment, especially where safety-sensitive work is involved.

stress-resilience.title: Movement and breaks
stress-resilience.explanation: Appropriate movement and breaks can support wellbeing, but ability, health, work conditions, and safety matter. A universal exercise target is not suitable advice for every learner.
stress-resilience.application: A fictional learner chooses a comfortable permitted break and notes its effect on attention.
stress-resilience.check: Adapt to personal circumstances and qualified guidance rather than pushing through pain or unsafe conditions.

stress-resilience.title: Thoughts versus facts
stress-resilience.explanation: A thought can be meaningful without being an established fact. Examining evidence can produce a more balanced interpretation without denying a real difficulty.
stress-resilience.application: A fictional 'I always fail' conclusion is compared with the actual missed task and occasions when follow-through occurred.
stress-resilience.check: Use evidence both for and against the thought instead of replacing it with an unsupported positive promise.

stress-resilience.title: Small wins
stress-resilience.explanation: A small win is a completed action or demonstrated skill, not proof that every larger barrier is solved. Specific recognition can make progress easier to see.
stress-resilience.application: A learner records one accurate application completed and one remaining document problem separately.
stress-resilience.check: Notice progress honestly while keeping the next unresolved step visible.

stress-resilience.title: Support requests
